en.title: House of the Dragon Just Made a Book Change With Real-World Echoes
en.summary: Rhaenyra Targaryen's actions in the Season 3 finale have irrevocably altered the political landscape of Westeros. This shocking departure from the books is deeply rooted in historical conflicts between church and state.
en.body:
In a move that sent shockwaves through Westeros and its viewership alike, **Rhaenyra Targaryen** made a pivotal decision in the **House of the Dragon** Season 3 finale that dramatically diverges from George R.R. Martin's source material. The Queen, in her escalating quest for power, ordered **Alyn of Hull** to assassinate the High Septon of King's Landing. This act, unprecedented in the lore, represents a radical severing of ties between the secular Targaryen crown and the spiritual authority of the Faith of the Seven.

The High Septon himself warned of the dire consequences, stating, "I am the High Septon of the Faith. To harm me is to declare war on the Starry Sept, to damn your soul to the deepest of the Seven Hells!" Yet, Rhaenyra, embracing a persona that transcends mortal rules, convinced Alyn by asserting his Valyrian bloodline, thus placing him above the laws of men and gods. This bold, almost sacrilegious act is a cornerstone of Rhaenyra's increasingly messianic self-perception, culminating in her proclamation to the smallfolk and court that she is the "Prince That Was Promised."

## A Historical Parallel Emerges

This dramatic shift in **House of the Dragon** is not merely a narrative flourish; it directly mirrors one of the most tumultuous periods in medieval European history: the Investiture Controversy. This prolonged struggle, primarily between the Holy Roman Emperors and the Papacy in the 11th and 12th centuries, revolved around who held the ultimate authority – the temporal power of kings or the spiritual power of the Pope. The conflict saw excommunications, political maneuvering, and even bloodshed as both sides vied for dominance.

The show's decision to have Rhaenyra eliminate the High Septon is a potent fictional echo of this real-world historical tension. It signifies a decisive moment where secular power, embodied by the Targaryen dynasty, chooses to forcibly assert its supremacy over religious institutions, a path that was fraught with peril and instability in reality. The showrunners have thus amplified the underlying political currents of Westeros, grounding the fantastical conflict in the very real, often brutal, power struggles that shaped our own past.

## The Stakes for the Realm

For fans who devour every detail of Westerosi politics, this change is monumental. It signifies that **House of the Dragon** is willing to take significant liberties with **Fire & Blood** to explore thematic depth and create compelling television. Rhaenyra's actions have not only alienated a powerful religious faction but have also potentially opened the door for further conflict, not just with the Faith but with any lords who hold religious convictions dear. This move elevates the stakes for her reign, presenting her not just as a queen fighting for her throne, but as a ruler willing to dismantle established orders for her own vision of control.

## What's Next

The consequences of Rhaenyra's defiance will undoubtedly unfold in future seasons, as the Faith's reaction and the loyalty of the lords hang precariously in the balance. Details regarding the next season's premiere date have not yet been announced.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for House of the Dragon Season 3 . Power resides where men believe it resides. This famous nugget of wisdom, spoken between Lord Varys and the Imp of Casterly Rock, is virtually a thesis statement for Game of Thrones and the larger George R.R. Martin universe. However, it also speaks to one of the most turbulent, and occasionally blood-soaked, political struggles that persisted throughout Europe’s actual medieval period: the balance for control between church and state. That tenuous see-saw action has played a major role in both Game of Thrones and its prequel series House of the Dragon , but never more so than in the latter’s season 3 finale . For it was in this climactic hour that Rhaenyra Targaryen, First of Her Name, took a step that her literary counterpart would never dare: she ordered Alyn of Hull to essentially assassinate the ranking septon who served in King’s Landing. In effect, she’s burned the bridge between the secular world of Targaryen kings and queens and the ecclesial one presided over by powerful priests. It’s an stunning murder that even Alyn hesitates committing. As the holy man in question warns, “I am the High Septon of the Faith. To harm me is to declare war on the Starry Sept, to damn your soul to the deepest of the Seven Hells!” Yet Alyn reluctantly takes Rhaenyra’s command to heart, as she soothes his doubts by telling him he is the blood of Old Valyria, and thus unburdened by the rules that govern men or the Seven-Faced Gods. It’s part and parcel for the entire power trip Rhaenyra is on in the finale, complete by announcing to thousands of gathered King’s Landing smallfolk and royal attendants that she is a savior-like figure foretold by her father and Aegon the Conqueror; “the Prince That Was Promised” who will redeem Westeros from the threat of monstrous evils far to the North and beyond the Wall! For the record, none of this happens in the book , so the ramifications for what it would mean for Rhaenyra and Westeros are profound. But before folks start drawing their pitchforks and torches for showrunner Ryan Condal and the House of the Dragon writing team, know that like the best shocks and twists in the “A Song of Ice and Fire” saga and Fire & Blood , the latter of which serves as the inspiration for House of the Dragon , this development has real-world precedent. Aye, the series seems to be adapting to its own purposes one of the most infamous scandals in English history whereupon a 12th century king ordered the murder of his former best friend, the Archbishop of Canterbury. A Kingsman Kills God’s Man The king and archbishop in question were Henry of House Plantagenet, a.k.a. Henry II, and Thomas Becket, and they were in fact once thick as thieves before Henry handpicked his drinking buddy to be the most authoritative voice of God on Earth, at least this side of the English Channel.
